answer:
**Final hypothesis (data-grounded):** 

"Age has a **modest negative association** with the probability of dissaving (DISSAVED=1) in this NLSY79 sample. Among respondents aged 24–32 in 1989, each additional year of age is associated with roughly a **0.75 percentage-point lower** predicted probability of having withdrawn more from savings than put in, net of income, gender, and race (adjusted logit AGE coef −0.0417, SE 0.0092, p≈5e-6; OR ≈ 0.96 per year; average marginal effect −0.0075). Predicted dissave rates fall from **~26.5% at age 24 to ~20.5% at age 32 (−22% relative, −6 pp)** over the 24–32 window; the gradient is almost identical with or without controls (income/gender/race barely attenuate it) and holds within both genders (women −0.035, p=0.007; men −0.049, p=0.0002; interaction p=0.41 — no significant sex difference). The decline is essentially linear across 24–32, with at most mild acceleration among 30–32-year-olds (quadratic p≈0.046; bucketed 30–32 coefficient −0.25 vs −0.03 for 27–29; BIC slightly favors the simpler linear model). **Important caveat — the association is fragile under data-integrity checks:** it is concentrated in the ~31% of rows where INCOME equals the sample mean (3,963 rows, most of which are also duplicated rows) — within those rows dissave rates fall steeply with age (16.3% → 11.6% → 7.0%), whereas in the clean-income subsample they are flat (28.0/29.8/29.6%). Excluding the mean-imputed income rows, the duplicates, or both, the age gradient attenuates to ~0 (coefs +0.012, +0.015, +0.001; all n.s.). The unadjusted and adjusted full-sample estimates are robust to adding SAMESAVE or BMI, but not to removing the imputed/duplicate rows. **Interpretation:** taken at face value the pattern is consistent with declining present-orientation (dissaving as a reveal-preference proxy for impatience) with age in young adulthood, but because this is a single observational 1989 cross-section limited to ages 24–32, with clearly constructed/imputed features, we can state only a *tentative modest negative association in this window*, not a causal or extrapolated claim."

**Headline numbers to carry forward:** headline adjusted OR/yr = 0.959 (per +1 year), AME = −0.0075, predicted P(DISSAVED) 24/27/30/32 = 0.265/0.242/0.219/0.206; unadjusted ≈ identical (0.266→0.205); gradient present in both genders; concentrated in imputed-income/duplicate rows and attenuated to ~0 in the clean subsample.

payload.hypothesis: Age is modestly negatively associated with the probability of DISSAVED=1 (withdrawing more than putting into savings) among 1989 NLSY79 respondents aged 24-32: net of income, gender, and race, each additional year of age predicts ~0.75 pp lower dissave probability (OR/yr~0.96; pred P ~26.5% at 24 to ~20.5% at 32, ~-22% relative); the gradient is near-identical with or without controls, present in both genders, essentially linear across the window, and consistent with declining present-orientation with age - but it is concentrated in mean-imputed-income/duplicate rows and attenuates to ~0 in the clean subsample, so it is a tentative pattern in this observational cross-section, not a robust causal or extrapolated effect.
payload.workflow: 1) Inspected nls_bmi_processed.csv (12,686x9, no missing; verified race reference groups non-overlapping; flagged 31.2% mean-imputed INCOME, 167 topcoded, 2,275 duplicate rows). 2) Fitted logistic regressions in statsmodels: unadjusted linear AGE vs headline adjusted (AGE centered + INCOME + FEMALE + BLACK + HISPANIC) vs +quadratic vs age-bucketed. 3) Reported average marginal effect (+1yr age = -0.0075) and average predicted probabilities at ages 24/27/30/32. 4) Linearity tests: LR bucketed p=0.054, quadratic p=0.046; BIC prefers linear. 5) Sensitivities: excluded mean-imputed income, imputed+topcoded, duplicate rows, implausible BMI; added SAMESAVE or BMI; gender-stratified + interaction. 6) Decomposed dissave-by-age by subsample to locate the gradient (imputed rows). All in final_analysis.py; outputs in results_summary.txt.
